title: Iran–Contra affair
wiki_lead:
The Iran–Contra affair or Iran–Contra scandal (Persian: ماجرای ایران-کنترا, also referred to as the Iran Initiative or Contragate, was a political scandal in the United States that centered on arms trafficking to Iran between 1981 and 1986, facilitated by senior officials of the Reagan administration. The administration hoped to use the proceeds of the arms sale to fund the Contras, an anti-Sandinista rebel group in Nicaragua. Under the Boland Amendments, a series of laws passed by Congress and signed by Ronald Reagan, further funding of the Contras by legislative appropriations was prohibited by Congress, but the Reagan administration continued funding them secretly using non-appropriated funds.
The administration's justification for the arms shipments was that they were part of an attempt to free seven U.S. hostages being held in Lebanon by Hezbollah, an Islamist paramilitary group connected to Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. The idea to exchange arms for hostages was proposed by Manucher Ghorbanifar, an expatriate Iranian arms dealer. Some within the Reagan administration hoped the sales would influence Iran to get Hezbollah to release the hostages.
After the Lebanese Magazine Ash-Shiraa reported on the weapon dealings in November 1986, it broke international news, prompting Reagan to appear on national television. He claimed that while the weapons transfers had indeed occurred, the U.S. did not trade arms for hostages. The investigation was impeded when large volumes of documents relating to the affair were destroyed or withheld from investigators by Reagan administration officials. In March 1987, Reagan made a further nationally televised address, saying he was taking full responsibility for the affair and stating that "what began as a strategic opening to Iran deteriorated, in its implementation, into trading arms for hostages."
The affair was investigated by Congress and by the three-person, Reagan-appointed Tower Commission. Neither investigation found evidence that President Reagan himself knew of the extent of the multiple programs. Additionally, U.S. deputy attorney general Lawrence Walsh was appointed independent counsel in December 1986 to investigate possible criminal actions by officials involved in the scheme. In the end, several dozen administration officials were indicted, including Secretary of Defense Caspar Weinberger and Lieutenant Colonel Oliver North. Eleven convictions resulted, some of which were vacated on appeal. The rest of those indicted or convicted were all pardoned in the final days of the presidency of George H. W. Bush, who had been vice president at the time of the affair. Only one Iran–Contra defendant, Thomas G. Clines, served a prison sentence; all of the others either received probation or were pardoned while their trials were still pending. Former Independent Counsel Walsh noted that, in issuing the pardons, Bush appeared to be preempting being implicated himself by evidence that came to light during the Weinberger trial, and that there was a pattern of "deception and obstruction" by Bush, Weinberger, and other senior Reagan administration officials. Walsh submitted his final report on 4 August 1993 and later wrote an account of his experiences as counsel, Firewall: The Iran-Contra Conspiracy and Cover-Up.

Key figures included NSC aide Lt. Col. Oliver North, who coordinated logistics with private intermediaries like Richard Secord, and national security advisers Robert McFarlane and John Poindexter, who approved the diversions totaling at least $3.8 million from the approximately $48 million in arms sale proceeds. The scandal erupted publicly in November 1986 following revelations in Lebanese media of the Iranian arms deals, prompting President Reagan to appoint the Tower Commission, whose February 1987 report criticized chaotic White House management and overreach by NSC personnel but found no conclusive evidence that Reagan had prior knowledge of the fund diversions, attributing the lapses to a flawed advisory process rather than deliberate lawbreaking by the president. Subsequent congressional joint hearings and independent counsel investigations uncovered operational details and led to convictions of several officials, including North and Poindexter, for misleading Congress and obstructing justiceâthough many were later overturned or pardonedâhighlighting tensions between executive foreign policy prerogatives and legislative oversight amid Cold War imperatives to counter Soviet influence in Central America and the Middle East.
